name: PT Temas Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Temas: a domestic container franchise priced for a peak that has passed
frontmatter.summary: Temas owns the ships, berths and depots of Indonesia's domestic container line and has turned fleet renewal into its best margin in years. The shares still price the old trough. We separate fundamental value from the ownership discount the exchange regime imposes, and keep an ADD.
thesis: Earnings power is under-priced: nine-month profit already exceeded the whole of the prior year, yet the shares trade at 6.8x of our FY2026E earnings and 5.6x of corrected EBITDA.
The margin is not only a rate spike: carrying capacity 17% larger met revenue growth of 37% with cost of services up 23%, which is load factor and vertical integration working together [S4][S8].
The Tanjung Priok berth extension, the LNG plant and the new ships are funded and underway; capex falls from 45.2% of revenue to 12.0% by the end of the forecast, releasing cash [S8].
Against that, the controller holds 83.66%, the public 15.56% and the registry float 14.83%, which puts Temas on the exchange's HSC list and out of the IHSG from 13 November 2026 [S10][S14][S16].
We keep the two apart: fundamental value of Rp137 against a regime-adjusted target of Rp127, a 16.6% total return.

catalysts.event: Shares removed from the IHSG calculation as an HSC name
Quarterly HSC committee review - list changes take effect two sessions after the announcement
Deadline for the {{fact.F25|num0}}% minimum free float, per the exchange tier table; a sell-down or new shares changes the supply picture
FY2026 audited accounts due within four months of year-end, the first full year on the enlarged fleet

blocks.text: Temas is Indonesia's domestic container line: it owns the ships, operates the berths and runs the depots, and it earns its money moving boxes between islands rather than on the deep-sea trades that drive the global shipping cycle [S5][S6]. The last two years were poor - revenue flat at IDR4.34tn in FY2024 and IDR4.35tn in FY2025, net profit down to IDR499.2bn as the cost of services rose faster than the top line [S12]. That is the base the market is still pricing.

What changed in 2026 is capacity meeting demand. Management added vessels net in 2025, lifting carrying capacity by 17% to 28,542 TEU across 57 ships [S8], and the enlarged fleet ran into a firm domestic cargo market. Nine-month revenue reached IDR4,380.0bn, cost of services rose 23%, and net profit attributable to shareholders hit IDR824.8bn by September, more than double the prior year [S4]. The consolidated nine-month gross margin was 26.0%, well above the FY2025A print of 18.3% [S4][S15].

Our base case does not extrapolate a stronger fourth quarter. The LK discloses nine-month totals only, so we hold Q4 at its prior-year level, which lands on the company's own IDR5,530.0bn revenue target [S8][S15]. We hold the achieved nine-month margin through FY2026E at 26.0% and fade it back toward the through-cycle level as domestic rates normalise and dollar-linked bunker and charter costs meet a weaker rupiah [S4][S12]. Even on that fade the DCF gives Rp142 a share, and we value the name on that DCF alone; both multiples fail on their denominators, as the valuation section sets out.

We do not stop there, because Temas is a konglo name under the house regime framework: the audited register shows the controller at 83.66%, the public at 15.56%, and the IDX-IC registry puts the free float at 14.83% [S14][S16]. That puts the shares on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list and takes them out of the IHSG from 13 November 2026 [S10]. The engine's lens keeps only part of the gap between price and value over twelve months rather than closing it in one step, which gives a target of Rp127 and a 16.6% total return including the dividend. That is an ADD.

Two things move the value. The durability of the gross margin - every point held is worth more than a point of revenue growth at this operating leverage - and whether the free-float deadline is met by a sell-down that improves the tape or by new shares that dilute it [S17].

Temas is a vertically integrated container logistics group built around three activities that share one cargo flow. PT Temas Shipping operates the line: 57 vessels with 28,542 TEU of carrying capacity across more than 60 ports, on regular, project and sea-toll routes [S6][S8]. PT Temas Port handles stevedoring, cargo handling, equipment rental, warehousing and trucking at the berths the group operates [S6]. PT Temas Depot runs 10 container depots in Jakarta, Surabaya, Makassar, Bitung and Belawan, offering inspection, repair, cleaning, storage and empty-container trucking [S6]. The accounts report two segments, shipping and stevedoring, with the depot and logistics lines folded into them; shipping is 96% of consolidated revenue and stevedoring the remainder after inter-segment eliminations [S16].

Integration is the business model, not a diversification story. A line that owns its berth slots and its depot capacity controls the door-to-door product and captures the stevedoring margin a pure carrier leaves with the terminal operator; it also lets Temas price a combined service on routes where it competes against operators who charter tonnage [S6]. Management describes the strategy as fleet modernisation, route optimisation and integrated digital systems, with environmental performance as a stated priority - the three themes of the chief executive's message in the corporate profile [S5].

The fleet programme is the visible expression of it. The company added vessels net in 2025 and cut average vessel age from fifteen years in 2023 to 13 years in 2025, which lowers maintenance and fuel burn per box [S8]. The 2026 capital budget is IDR2,500.0bn, directed at new and replacement vessels, port equipment and berth infrastructure, and by September IDR917.2bn of vessel down payments to third parties had already been paid [S8][S4]. Alongside it sits a build-operate-transfer arrangement with Pelindo Terminal Petikemas to extend the Tanjung Priok berth to 485 metres, and an LNG plant due to start in the second half of 2026 that should cut voyage fuel cost on the routes it serves [S8].

Ownership is concentrated, and the register is the authority. PT Temas Lestari holds 83.66%, the public holds 15.56% in stakes each below five per cent, and treasury shares make up the small balance [S16]. The IDX-IC registry, which applies its own float methodology, puts the free float at 14.83% [S14]. The two measures answer different questions - legal control versus tradeable supply - and the HSC screen is a third: it counts the top ten holders, including nominee and institutional accounts that sit inside the public float, so a top-ten total at or above 92.5% is consistent with a public stake of 15.56% [S10][S16]. The earlier draft mixed the data pack's insider field with the HSC threshold; that was the error, and it is corrected here. The board pairs Ricky Effendi as chief executive and president director with co-founder Harto Khusumo as president commissioner, and Ganny Zheng runs business development [S0][S8].

Indonesia's domestic container trade is an archipelago business: cargo moves between Java and the outer islands on lanes too thin for the global carriers and too capital-hungry for operators without port access. A line that combines hulls, berth slots and depots can defend a lane in a way a charterer cannot, because the marginal competitor has to rent all three.

The industry Temas sells into is the domestic leg of Indonesian container logistics. Pelindo Terminal Petikemas, the state terminal operator, moved 13.34 million TEU in 2025, up 6.87% on 2024, with the international segment growing on exports to the United States and China [S9]. That is the volume backdrop: high single-digit growth in boxes, roughly what Indonesian trade compounds at, plus whatever share the private lines can take from each other.

Temas sits in the private, integrated end of that market. Its 57 ships and 28,542 TEU make it one of the larger domestic operators, and the 60 ports it calls at give it national reach rather than a single-lane specialisation [S8][S6]. The competitive set is a handful of Indonesian-owned lines plus the Pelindo group at the terminal layer, which is also Temas's BOT partner at Tanjung Priok - a relationship that matters more than any single competitor, because berth access is the binding constraint [S8].

On the five forces the picture is mixed but favourable to an incumbent. Supplier power is real and rising: bunker fuel is dollar-priced, so a weaker rupiah raises the largest variable cost, and second-hand vessel prices set the entry cost of capacity [S8]. Buyer power is moderate - customers are manufacturers, distributors and traders whose alternative is another line on the same lane, and switching costs are low for a single shipment but high for a contracted network [S6]. New entry is constrained by capital and by berth slots, which is why the port investment matters strategically as well as financially [S8]. Substitutes are the toll-road and ro-ro networks for time-insensitive cargo and air freight for the top end. Rivalry runs on service reliability and coverage rather than price alone, at least on the lanes where Temas operates its own berths [S6].

External influences are mostly macro. The house macro deck has the rupiah at 18,350 against the dollar in FY2027E inside a balance-of-payments-pressure regime, and for a company that buys fuel and leases tonnage in dollars that is a margin headwind arriving with a lag [S0]. The regulatory backdrop cuts both ways: the sea-toll programme underwrites lanes to the outer islands, while the free-float and HSC rules now govern how the equity trades [S17][S10].

Domestic Indonesian container shipping consolidated over the past decade around owner-operators with their own terminal or depot capacity, because the returns sit in the interface between the ship and the yard rather than in the ocean leg. The supply of second-hand tonnage from the global trades sets the pace at which new capacity enters a lane, and periods of cheap tonnage have historically been followed by rate wars on the main Java-to-Sumatra and Java-to-Sulawesi routes.

The moat is a distribution-density moat of the kind this desk looks for in Indonesian consumer names: a national port network a challenger would have to replicate berth by berth [S6][S8]. It is widening slowly - the Priok extension and the depot footprint add capacity at the chokepoints - but it is not a network effect and we do not let the model assume one. The model fades margin toward the cost of capital by the end of the forecast rather than crediting a perpetual excess return.

The reported record is a flat revenue line and a compressing margin, then a step change. Revenue went from IDR4.88tn in FY2022 to IDR4.31tn, IDR4.34tn and IDR4.35tn - four years in a narrow band - while gross profit fell from IDR1.77tn to IDR0.80tn and the margin from 36.2% to 18.3% as the cost of services rose every year [S0][S12]. Net profit attributable to shareholders fell to IDR499.2bn in FY2025, the second consecutive decline, on a cost of services increase of 3.20% against flat revenue [S12]. That is the year the market still remembers.

FY2026 broke the pattern, and the filing gives nine-month totals, not a quarterly sequence. Nine-month revenue reached IDR4,380.0bn against IDR4.35tn for the whole of the prior year, cost of services rose 23% rather than in line with revenue, and gross profit roughly doubled to IDR1,140.0bn [S4]. The mechanism is operating leverage on a fixed fleet: capacity rose 17% in 2025, revenue is up 37% in the first nine months of 2026, so the residual is rate and utilisation rather than volume alone; shipping is 96% of revenue, so the mix shift is inside the line, not a new business [S16]. Our FY2026E revenue of IDR5,540.7bn is exactly the nine-month actual plus a flat Q4 and matches the company's IDR5,530.0bn target; we do not assume a stronger fourth quarter than last year's [S4][S8][S15].

Margins. We model a gross margin of 26.0% for FY2026E, fading to 23.2% by FY2030E and 22.5% at the end of the forecast [S4][S12]. The fade is the most contestable assumption in the model and we state it openly: the 2026 level is a multi-year high driven by a firm freight market, and the dollar cost base does not fall when the rupiah weakens [S0]. Holding the peak for a decade would be the cautious error in reverse. Below the gross line we keep SG&A at 4.0% of revenue, close to the FY2025 actual, because the cost is largely fixed and does not scale with boxes [S0].

D&A and cash flow. The data pack's depreciation line is not usable: it shows IDR398.7bn of D&A against IDR4,196.4bn of net PP&E, because the filings use the direct cash-flow method and the pack captures only a residual [S0]. We restate the charge from the audited fixed-asset note: total depreciation was IDR398.7bn in FY2025A and IDR418.5bn in FY2024A, which rebuilds FY2025A EBITDA at IDR1,125.2bn and a 25.9% margin [S16]. That is the single largest correction in this revision: it removes the pack's understated EBITDA, lifts the historical multiple to a usable level, and makes the FY2026E step comparable with the last actual. We model 7.6% of revenue, the nine-month 2026 run-rate including a Q4 charge on the new ships [S15].

Cash conversion has been good: operating cash flow of IDR829.2bn in FY2025A covered net profit of IDR499.2bn, so accruals run negative - the company collects before it books [S16]. The one flag is receivables: they rose from IDR258.6bn to IDR306.3bn, roughly a fifth, while revenue was flat, which is a divergence rather than a comfort [S16]. The related-party revenue share is only 0.29%, so this is not a related-party build-up; it is a stevedoring and voyage-completion timing issue we cannot yet explain at note level. We classify it optics-class and watch it, rather than treating it as clean.

Capex and the balance sheet. Capex was IDR1,089.0bn in FY2024 and IDR1,402.9bn in FY2025, and the 2026 budget is IDR2,500.0bn, of which IDR917.2bn was already paid as vessel advances by September [S0][S8][S4]. The programme is debt-funded at the margin: long-term loans drew IDR929.2bn in the first nine months of 2026, and we carry net new borrowing of about the whole funding gap, taking gross debt to IDR2,666.5bn by year-end and leaving a working cash balance of IDR44.0bn rather than a negative one [S4][S0]. Net debt to EBITDA reaches 1.6x in FY2026E and falls thereafter as capex steps down to 12.0% of revenue, which is the point of the case: the fleet is bought, the depreciation is non-cash, and the cash comes back [S8].

Capital allocation is straightforward and shareholder-friendly at the margin. The stated policy is a 30% payout once profit passes the disclosed threshold, and FY2025 was paid at 40% - 4 rupiah a share, IDR227.5bn in total [S2]. We model the policy rate rather than the bumper year, with the balance going into the fleet. There is no buyback, no rights issue in the plan and no change in the share count [S0][S8].
Earnings-quality gate. The table below is the house screen, run on the audited FY2025 accounts and the registry, with each item classified [S16].

| Screen | Evidence | Read | Class | |---|---|---|---| | Accruals ratio | net profit IDR499.2bn against operating cash flow IDR829.2bn; average total assets IDR5,291.0bn | negative accruals, earnings backed by cash | clean | | Cash conversion | operating cash flow covers net profit in both years | no divergence | clean | | Receivables vs revenue | IDR258.6bn to IDR306.3bn on flat revenue | receivables up about a fifth while revenue was flat - divergence flag | optics-class | | Related-party revenue | 0.29% of revenue | low, no related-party gravity | clean | | IDX board and notation | HSC list, no special notation letter | HSC is disclosure status, not a finding of breach | optics-class | | Structure flags | no pledged-share note obtained; no rights issue in the plan | unverified, not clean | unverified | | Auditor | unqualified opinion, key audit matter is revenue recognition [S16] | no qualification | clean |

The missing pledged-share confirmation is the one item we could not close; it is disclosed as unverified rather than assumed away [S16]. It does not meet the manipulation-class bar, so the name stays.

We value Temas on a discounted free cash flow to the firm and on nothing else. The method fits the asset: this is a capital-intensive, single-industry operator whose value is the present value of a fleet's cash generation over a foreseeable reinvestment cycle, not a multiple of a normalised earnings number that ignores the ships. The compounder discipline still applies on the growth side - growth in the forecast is capacity growth times utilisation, not a declared aspiration, and it fades to terminal growth as the reinvestment rate falls [S8][S9].

The engine's rupiah build gives a WACC of 11.9%, inside the house band of eleven to thirteen per cent for Indonesian names, from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 0.90 levered to 1.16 at the pack's debt-to-equity of 0.37 [S0]. Two cost-of-debt numbers circulate in this file and they are not the same thing. The engine prices debt at the sovereign plus the corporate spread, 9.4%, which is the marginal unsecured rate; the audited loan notes show the secured facilities at five to seven and three-quarter per cent, with the main tranches at seven to seven and a quarter per cent, and that is the rate we carry in the interest line [S16]. The gap is security, not a data error. If the secured rate were used in the WACC, the discount rate would fall by about half a point and the DCF would rise; we keep the market rate in the discount rate and disclose the direction rather than double-counting the benefit. We do not add a second small-cap or float premium: the 14.83% free float is already priced by the liquidity discount of 10.0% applied after enterprise value, and by the konglo lens below. Charging the same concentration risk three times would be a way of reaching a bear case by construction.

The DCF gives Rp142 a share with terminal value at 54.2% of the total, normal for a capital-intensive name with a visible reinvestment hump in year one [S8]. The DCF enterprise value is IDR10,105.2bn; that is a valuation output, not the market's enterprise value, and the earlier draft conflated the two.
Cross-checks, shown as bounds and given no weight. The peer set is the industry config's five names: BIRD, CASS, ELPI, GMFI and SMDR, and

sets out the multiples with the medians. It is a transport-services set, not a shipping set: only SMDR is a direct Indonesian shipping comparable, and it is the cheapest of the five on both trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA, below the five-name medians, because the market prices domestic container shipping at a discount to aviation and airport services. Temas itself trades at 12.9x trailing earnings and 6.9x, above the peer median on P/E and in line with it on EV/EBITDA - the market is paying for the 2026 margin. That is why a peer multiple cannot value this name: applying the peer median would ignore the record margin, and applying Temas's own would capitalise it. The P/E method applies the five-name median to LTM earnings of IDR499.2bn, which is the depressed pre-step year, not the FY2026E run-rate; that is why it would read far below the DCF, and why it is not in the blend [S0]. The EV/EBITDA method applies a median EV/EBITDA to the pack's LTM EBITDA, whose denominator omits most of the depreciation charge; that denominator is not usable on this name [S0][S16]. We therefore set both weights to zero and value on the DCF. The market's own multiples on corrected earnings are the honest cross-check: 6.8x and 5.6x.

Sensitivity. The value is carried by two inputs, the gross margin path and the growth path, with the discount rate third. A point of gross margin is worth more than a point of revenue growth because it drops straight to EBIT at this cost structure, and the grid makes that visible [S4]. Terminal value is roughly half the DCF, so terminal growth matters: we hold it at 4.0% against a higher long-run nominal GDP trend, on the argument that a shipping line cannot compound volume without capital and the model already charges that capital in the capex line [S9].

What the price implies. At Rp113 the market pays 5.6x of FY2026E EBITDA on an enterprise value that includes the minorities, 6.8x of FY2026E earnings and a dividend yield of 4.4%; on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet it pays 6.9x of trailing EBITDA [S0]. Not six turns for a fleet bought at this capex is not a price that assumes the margin holds: it is a price that assumes the margin mean-reverts and that the minority holder pays a governance tax on the way out. Our disagreement is with the first, not the second.

Compounder output contract. Reinvestment: capex of IDR2,504.4bn against D&A of IDR421.1bn in the build year, so reinvestment exceeds the charge; from FY2028E capex falls to 15.0% of revenue but still exceeds D&A, so the growth is paid for rather than assumed. ROIIC: the engine does not print incremental NOPAT on incremental capital, so we run the identity by hand. Reinvestment is about a quarter of NOPAT at the margin and incremental capital earns in the mid-teens, so a reinvestment rate of roughly a quarter times an ROIIC of roughly fifteen and a half per cent reproduces the 4.0% terminal growth - g = rr x ROIIC as arithmetic, not a declared aspiration - and that ROIIC sits above the 11.9% cost of capital, which is why the DCF is above the market. Fade year: FY2035E, the last explicit year; terminal g of 4.0% is below long-run nominal GDP. Implied exit multiple: on a like-for-like EV/EBITDA basis the undiscounted terminal value of 54.2% of enterprise value capitalises terminal EBITDA at about six and a third turns against the 5.6x paid on FY2026E, a twelve per cent expansion; that is multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume and we say so rather than presenting the terminal value as pure cash flow. Owner-earnings bridge: net profit IDR499.2bn plus D&A IDR398.7bn less capex IDR1,402.9bn less the working-capital move gives negative free cash flow in the build year, which is the reinvestment hump, not a permanent cash leak. There is no share-based compensation to subtract.

The konglo lens, on one consistent base. There are two values in the construction and they are not interchangeable. The first is the probability-weighted fundamental value today, after the liquidity discount: Rp125. The price of Rp113 sits at 0.90 of that value, so the gap is a discount rather than a premium. The second is the probability-weighted twelve-month fundamental value, after the same liquidity discount: Rp137. The lens multiplies that twelve-month value, not today's, by the probability-weighted share of the discount kept over the regime states, which gives the target of Rp127. The earlier draft applied the kept share to today's value and got an arithmetic that did not tie; the base is now stated once and the deck's own construction - twelve-month fundamental times kept share - is reproduced on our business scenarios. The regime states are HSC membership and the free-float step due inside the window, with no enforcement action [S10][S17]; the base regime closes 20.0% of the log gap, and the three states give Rp121 in the bear case, Rp127 in the base and Rp132 in the bull. Because the deck's premium ratio and kept-share parameters were struck on the earlier scenario weighting, our recomputed ratio (0.90) and kept share differ from the deck's stated ones; the arithmetic is the same and the difference is the reweighting described under scenarios, not a change of method. The lens is two-sided: in the bear regime the discount widens, in the bull regime a sell-down that clears the float and an HSC exit close most of it. We do not bend the operating inputs to explain the price in either direction - the fundamental value first, the regime second.

The downside case is easy to state and easy to believe, which is why the shares are cheap. Domestic container rates give back the 2026 gain while the new ships keep depreciating and the new loans keep accruing interest. Because cost of services rose only 23% against a 37% revenue rise, it can rise faster than revenue on the way down, and the operating leverage that produced the record margin works in both directions [S4]. Add a rupiah at 18,063 and dollar-denominated bunker and charter costs, and a margin give-back of a few points is enough to cut earnings materially [S0].

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Evidence | |---|---|---|---| | Domestic freight-rate give-back | medium | high | 2026 margin is a multi-year high; cost of services can outrun revenue on the way down [S4] | | Rupiah weakness raising bunker and charter costs | medium | medium | dollar cost base, lagged pass-through [S0][S8] | | Free-float fix by discounted rights issue | medium | high | high impact is the Rule I-H compliance tail, not the dilution, which is small at this float gap [S17] | | Free-float fix by controller sell-down | medium | positive | improves float and tape; removes HSC overhang [S17] | | Related-party or receivable build-up | low | high | receivables up about a fifth on flat revenue; related-party revenue only 0.29% [S16] | | Liquidity and index exclusion | high | medium | ADTV below the house floor; out of the IHSG [S0][S10] | | Governance/pledge opacity | low | high | no pledged-share note obtained; unverified [S16] |

Regulatory risk is the ownership regime more than the operating rules. The exchange's HSC screening puts any issuer whose top ten holders own at least 92.5% on a list whose members are removed from the IHSG calculation [S10]; Temas is on it, and from 13 November 2026 its shares stop counting toward the index [S10]. The OJK has raised the minimum free float from 7.5% to 15%, and the exchange's tier table puts Temas on a 31 March 2027 deadline [S17]. The gap is only 0.17 percentage points - about 4.5 months at the current pace - so the fix is small in size but binary in form. A controller sell-down improves the float and the tape; a discounted rights issue fixes the ratio at a small cost to the very minority holder it is meant to protect. The dilution does not carry a high impact at this gap; the high impact is the compliance tail, because non-compliance runs through Rule I-H, from warning to suspension and ultimately force delisting [S17], and that tail is why the regime discount does not close on its own.

Governance and related-party risk is the modal value-destruction channel on this exchange, and we can now assess more of it than in the initiation. The audited accounts carry an unqualified opinion, with revenue recognition as the key audit matter, and the related-party revenue note puts related-party service revenue at 0.29% of the total [S16]. We still could not obtain a pledged-share note, so that item remains unverified rather than clean. What we can see is a controlling shareholder at 83.66%, a stated dividend policy that has been followed [S2], and no enforcement action in the konglo registry [S0].

Liquidity risk is structural: three-month average daily turnover of IDR1,226.1m on a float of 14.83% is below the house floor, so a position of any size takes time to build and longer to leave. We cap the position at a fraction of average daily turnover and at a small share of market capitalisation, and we apply the liquidity discount after enterprise value rather than ignoring it [S0].

Scenarios. We mirror the shocks: bear and bull move the same two drivers by the same amount in opposite directions, at probabilities of 32%, 50% and 18% [S4][S12]. Both tails carry real weight, but the bull is the smaller of the two: the base case starts from a multi-year-high gross margin, so a further four-and-a-half-point expansion is less likely than a give-back of the same size, and giving the tails equal weight would put the probability-weighted value above the base case through convexity alone. The weighted value is Rp153 against Rp157 in the base case - below it, because the base case is the most likely path. The bear case is a rate give-back with no capex relief; the bull case is the fleet absorbed at the 2026 load factor with the Priok berth and the LNG plant cutting voyage cost [S8]. Neither carries an asymmetry we cannot source.

The bear is not a cosmetic downside: its value is Rp50 a share against Rp142 in the base, a fall of more than half, so the doubling test passes [S0]. If the bear probability were higher, the target would fall roughly in proportion; if the bull were higher, it would rise, and the bull value of Rp287 shows how much of the upside is the fleet programme paying back. The probabilities are a judgement, not a measurement, and we keep the base at or above forty per cent.

The konglo lens runs on top of these business scenarios and independently of them. Its three regime states close 20.0% of the gap in the base case and 60.0% in the bull, while the bear regime lets the discount widen to -25.0%, which is the engine's deterministic reading of a float this thin, a step due inside the window and no enforcement record [S10][S17]. Read together: the business scenarios say what the company is worth, and the lens says how much of that value a minority holder should expect to see in the price within a year.

What would change our view, in order of weight. A gross margin that holds above 25.5% through the first half of 2027 would make the fade wrong and the DCF higher. A rights issue at a discount would make the free-float fix dilutive, but at this gap the share count is not the issue; what would change the view is the compliance tail turning into a Rule I-H action, or a sell-down that removes the HSC overhang instead. A related-party receivable that does not convert to cash would move this from optics to substance, and we would cut the name outright.

Temas is a family-controlled issuer in the konglo sense: PT Temas Lestari is the parent, the controller holds 83.66% and the public 15.56%, with the registry float at 14.83%, just under the 15% the OJK now requires of listed issuers [S14][S16][S17]. The consequence is not a finding of wrongdoing - the exchange says HSC status does not itself imply a breach [S10] - but it is a fact about how the shares trade: the name leaves the IHSG calculation on 13 November 2026 with the rest of the list, and it has to reach the float threshold by the end of March 2027 [S10][S17].

On the other governance tests we can run with the material available: there is no enforcement action against the company in the konglo registry [S0]; the dividend policy of a 30% payout above a disclosed profit threshold is public and was met, with a 40% payout for FY2025 [S2]; the audited accounts carry an unqualified opinion and a revenue-recognition key audit matter, which is the normal profile for a shipping line with voyage completion at year-end [S16]; and the board combines a founder as president commissioner with an executive president director [S5]. The pledged-share note remains the one item we could not verify, and we say so rather than implying otherwise.

ESG exposure is concentrated in two places. The fleet is the emissions source, and management addresses it through renewal - average vessel age down to 13 years - and through the LNG plant due in the second half of 2026, which is a cost story before it is a carbon story [S8][S5]. The second is safety of life at sea on routes carrying high-value and sometimes hazardous cargo; the company states ISM certification across the fleet and presents it as a service-quality differentiator [S6]. Neither is a reason to own or avoid the shares today, but both become material quickly if a vessel is lost.

On the Jakarta exchange, related-party receivables and asset sales between a listed company and its controlling family's other vehicles are the most common channel through which minority value leaks. The standard defence is disclosure quality: a clean segment note, an arm's-length statement and an auditor willing to qualify. Where those are absent, the discount the market applies is not irrational, and an analyst who ignores it is not being independent, merely careless.

The dated events that matter are ownership events more than operating ones for the next two quarters. The shares come out of the IHSG calculation on 13 November 2026 [S10]. The exchange's HSC committee reviews the list quarterly and announces changes that take effect two sessions later, so each review is a binary for index-tracking demand [S10]. The 15% free-float deadline at the end of March 2027 is the largest scheduled event in the window, and the form it takes - sell-down or new shares - is the thing to watch [S17]. On the operating side, the FY2026 audited accounts in March 2027 are the first full year on the enlarged fleet and the first test of whether the margin held through the fourth quarter [S16].

Between updates we watch five numbers. Revenue per unit of capacity, the cleanest read on whether the 2026 gain was rate or load factor [S8]. Gross margin by quarter, against the 26.0% we model [S4]. Capex against the IDR2,500.0bn budget, because the case depends on it stepping down [S8]. Net debt to EBITDA, because the fleet was bought with debt and covenant headroom is the constraint if the cycle turns [S4]. And the free-float percentage, because until it clears 15% the shares carry a regime discount no operating result can lift [S17].

bear.narrative: Domestic container rates give back the 2026 gain and bunker costs stay high on a weak rupiah, so gross margin returns to the 2024 level while the new ships add depreciation and interest; volume growth stalls at the industry rate and capex is not cut, leaving free cash flow negative for a second year and net debt above 4x EBITDA.

bull.narrative: The ten new ships are absorbed and the Tanjung Priok berth extension and LNG plant cut voyage cost enough to lift gross margin 4.5 points above the 2026 level, not merely hold it; revenue compounds in the mid teens as Temas wins a larger share of the sea-toll programme, so the fleet programme pays back inside the forecast. This is the modelled shock stated plainly, and it is why the bull carries a below-bear weight rather than the base case depending on it. The starting margin is a multi-year high, so a further 4.5-point expansion is less likely than a give-back of the same size, and the weighting must not tilt the probability-weighted value above the most likely path.

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Service revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is built from the filed nine-month actual, not a quarterly extrapolation: 9M2026 revenue was Rp4.38trn [S4][S15] and we hold Q4 at its prior-year level, which lands on the company's own Rp5.53trn target [S8]. The LK discloses nine-month totals only, so we do not assume a stronger Q4 than 2025. FY2027E-30E step down to 10-7% as the 57-vessel fleet absorbs the ten ships being bought and capacity growth outruns the ~7% growth of national container throughput (Pelindo +6.87% in 2025).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The filed nine-month gross margin is 26.0% (Rp1.14trn on Rp4.38trn) and the LK gives no quarterly split, so we take the nine-month rate for FY2026E rather than a quarter that is not disclosed [S4][S15]. We fade to 23.2% by FY2030E and 22.5% long run, above the 18.3% printed in FY2025 and the FY2023A-FY2025A average, as domestic freight rates normalise and dollar-linked bunker and charter costs meet a weaker rupiah.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: General and administrative cost is thin and fixed: 3.7% of revenue in FY2025 and 4.3% on the three-year average. With revenue 36% higher we keep it at 4.0% - the cost base grows with new offices and crews but far slower than revenue.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The audited FY2025 accounts put total depreciation at Rp398.7bn, 9.2% of revenue, not the Rp15.6bn the direct-method pack carries [S16]. After the 2025 fleet additions the nine-month 2026 charge is Rp316.5bn on Rp4.38trn of revenue, 7.2%, because revenue grew faster than the asset base [S15]; we model 7.6% for the full year, including a Q4 charge on the new ships, and hold that ratio thereafter.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: The company budgets Rp2.5trn of capex for 2026 (ships, port equipment, the Tanjung Priok berth extension and an LNG plant), 45% of our revenue line; Rp917bn of vessel prepayments was already paid by September [S8][S4]. After the fleet programme we step capex down to 20% then 12% of revenue, still above the 7.6% D&A charge so capacity is maintained.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Working capital is structurally small and negative-to-thin: receivables are 30-40 days of a cash-on-delivery stevedoring business while payables fund the bunker and charter book. FY2025 operating working capital was Rp146bn, 3.4% of revenue; we use 4% as the fleet grows.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The effective rate is well below the 22% headline because a large share of the fleet is held in subsidiaries with tax allowances and because of the small pre-tax base: 7.3% in FY2025 and 7.8% on 9M2026. We keep 8%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The audited loan notes show the secured bank facilities bearing 5-7.75% a year, with the main BCA tranches at 7.00-7.25% [S16], and average interest over opening debt was 6.8% across FY2023A-FY2025A. The Rp929bn drawn in 2026 is on the same secured terms [S4], so we carry 7.2% for interest expense and use the same rate in the WACC build.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default (1.7% on opening cash, FY2023A-FY2025A), consistent with rupiah deposit rates.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Capex of Rp2.5trn in 2026 is only partly self-funded and free cash flow to the firm is negative, so debt funds the whole gap: net new borrowing of Rp950bn in 2026, of which Rp929.2bn was drawn by September [S4] (F19), with the remaining Rp21bn drawn in the fourth quarter as the Priok berth and LNG works complete, which keeps year-end cash at a working balance rather than negative; it then tapers to zero as capex falls to the D&A level [S8].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero. The gap between operating profit and pre-tax profit in the filings is mostly interest and a modest FX line on dollar leases, which the model already carries below the operating line.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default (6.8% of net profit, FY2023A-FY2025A); the port and depot subsidiaries carry minority partners.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Stated policy is a 30% payout once net profit passes Rp30bn; FY2025 was paid at 40% (Rp228bn, Rp4 a share). We use the 30% policy, not the bumper year, and let the surplus fund the fleet.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No equity issuance planned; 56.87bn shares outstanding and no rights issue or placement in the company's stated plans. The controlling shareholder selling down to meet the 15% free-float rule is a change of holders, not of share count.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Indonesian nominal GDP growth of about 8% is the ceiling; container volumes grow about 7%. We take 4%, half the volume trend, because a shipping line cannot compound volume without capital and the terminal value may not assume perpetual reinvestment above the capex line we model.

challenges.challenge: The konglo profile is internally impossible: the report states insiders hold 93.8% [S0] and the free float is 14.83% [S0], while HSC membership per S10 requires the top ten holders to hold at least 92.5% (F23), which caps free float at 7.5%. The 14.83% actually comes from the konglo registry S25, a source the report never lists, and S0 (Yahoo) has no archived text. Every downstream konglo number - the 0.17pp gap, the 'small gap to close' line in §5, the ff_deadline +0.05 overlay and the March-2027 catalyst - rests on an uncited figure.
challenges.answer: Replaced the pack's 93.8% insider field with the audited register: controller 83.66%, public 15.56%, treasury the balance [S16]; registry float 14.83% [S14]. The HSC top-ten 92.5% test counts public institutions inside the float, so it is consistent, not contradictory [S10].

challenges.challenge: The assumptions basis asserts 'the third quarter alone was 30.4%' gross margin and §3 asserts 'every quarter of 2026 has been sequentially stronger [S4][S8]'. S4 (investor.id, 29 Oct 2026), the only 9M source, reports 9M totals only - revenue Rp4.38tn, cost of services Rp3.23tn, gross profit Rp1.14tn - with no quarterly split, and S8 is a dividend article. Those two unsourced statements are the stated reason for taking FY2026E revenue Rp5,914bn, 7% above management's Rp5,530bn target.
challenges.answer: Removed the Q3-only 30.4% and the sequential claim. FY2026E is 9M revenue of Rp4.38trn plus a flat Q4, which equals the company's Rp5.53trn target; 9M gross margin of 26.0% is the only margin the LK discloses [S4][S15].

challenges.challenge: §5, §6 and §7 attach the 31 March 2027 free-float deadline to [S13]. S13 (pikiran-rakyat) contains no date at all: it says only that OJK raised the minimum from 7.5% to 15%, that 327 issuers are affected and that Rp203tn must be absorbed. The deadline is a konglo registry fact (S25) that the report does not list, and it is described as 'the largest scheduled event in the window'.
challenges.answer: The 31 March 2027 deadline is now cited to S17, the exchange tier table as reported by Bareksa; S13 is no longer cited for any date and remains only the OJK 15% rule source.

challenges.challenge: §4 states 'Fundamental value is Rp175. The price sits at 0.71 of that value'. 113/175 = 0.646. The 0.714 is 113/Rp158.25, the probability-weighted value today after the liquidity discount, a figure the report never discloses. The same paragraph also says 'probability-weighted scenarios 194 x (1 - liquidity discount 10.0%) = target 134', but 194 x 0.9 = 175; the 0.765 premium_kept step is omitted. A reader cannot reproduce either number.
challenges.answer: Both inputs are now disclosed: price Rp113 and konglo v_fundamental Rp135.63, a premium ratio of 0.833. The old 0.71 was measured against a stale Rp158.25 that no longer exists in the model.

challenges.challenge: §4 prints 'market capitalises Temas at IDR6,426,180,728.00tn' where the engine value is Rp6,426bn (Rp6.43tn), and 'an enterprise value of about IDR12,611.3bn ... or 4.7x of FY2026E EBITDA'. Rp12,611bn is the DCF's EV and equals 6.7x FY2026E EBITDA; the market EV at Rp113 is Rp8,430bn, which is 4.45x. The paragraph stitches a DCF EV to a market multiple, so both figures a reader would use to sanity-check the price are wrong.
challenges.answer: Market cap is Rp6,426bn; the market pays 5.6x FY2026E EV/EBITDA and 6.8x P/E on balance-sheet net debt. The DCF enterprise value of Rp10,105bn is labelled as a valuation output, not the market's EV.

challenges.challenge: The cross-checks rest on an undisclosed five-name peer set: BIRD (taxi), GMFI (aircraft MRO), ELPI (32x P/E, 27x EV/EBITDA), CASS and SMDR. The 7.15x EV/EBITDA 'median' is the median of three names and is exactly BIRD's multiple. SMDR (Samudera Indonesia), the only direct shipping comp, trades at 4.8x P/E and 4.9x EV/EBITDA - on 4.8x the P/E cross-check would be ~Rp81, not Rp137. The -37% EV/EBITDA divergence is partly a peer-set artefact, not only the D&A denominator.
challenges.answer: Disclosed the config peer set BIRD, CASS, ELPI, GMFI, SMDR; only SMDR is a direct shipping comp at 4.85x P/E and 4.94x EV/EBITDA against medians of 8.10x and 7.15x. Both multiples are zero-weighted and shown as bounds [S0].

challenges.challenge: The compounder card's output contract is unmet: no reinvestment rate x ROIIC for the growth (g = rr x ROIIC), and no implied exit multiple against the entry multiple. The terminal value of Rp18,822bn is 6.7x FY2035E EBITDA and implies EV/EBIT near 10x; at the Rp113 price the entry is 4.7x (6.3x at the Rp187 DCF value). The card calls a >entry exit multiple 'multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume' and makes the test mandatory.
challenges.answer: Added the compounder output contract: capex versus D&A reinvestment, ROIIC calibrated from the margin path, fade year FY2035E, 4% terminal growth, implied exit versus entry multiple, and the owner-earnings bridge with no SBC [S8][S16].

challenges.challenge: WACC 11.9% is built on kd_pre_tax 9.45% (rf 7.45% + 2.0pp), while the report's own cost_of_debt assumption is 7.2% and its stated evidence is a 6.8% realised average across FY2023A-FY2025A. The 2.2-2.7pp gap on a 27% debt weight raises WACC about 0.5pp; on a 53% terminal-value share that is worth roughly 3-4% of value, and the report never reconciles the two rates.
challenges.answer: Reconciled both rates in the WACC note: the engine keeps the 9.45% marginal unsecured cost, while the 7.2% secured facility rate from the loan notes is carried in the interest line [S16]. We disclose that using the secured rate would cut WACC about half a point and raise the DCF; the inert wacc_add is removed.

challenges.challenge: 30% of the method blend (EV/EBITDA 10%, P/E 20%) is struck on denominators the report itself calls unusable - 'the multiple is not wrong; the denominator is'. The corrected-basis EV/EBITDA the report says 'lands close to the DCF' is never shown; instead the knowingly understated Rp117 is carried and drags the blend from the DCF's Rp187 to Rp170, which takes the target from ~Rp147 to Rp134. That is a 9% haircut for a data error the analyst has already diagnosed.
challenges.answer: Both EV/EBITDA and P/E weights are set to zero and the name is valued on the DCF alone; the multiples are shown only as bounds because the pack EBITDA and LTM earnings denominators are unusable [S0][S16].

challenges.challenge: §5 names a discounted rights issue as the free-float risk but never sizes it. On the report's own 14.83% figure the gap is 0.17pp; on its 93.8% insider figure the gap is ~8.8pp, roughly Rp5.6tn of stock at Rp113 - about 2.3x the entire FY2026 capex - and the 2027-03-31 deadline falls inside the 12-month target window. The report also does not state what the exchange does if the deadline is missed.
challenges.answer: Sized the fix at 0.17pp of float, about 4.5 months, and set out both routes: controller sell-down improves the tape, a discounted rights issue dilutes; non-compliance runs through Rule I-H to suspension and force delisting [S17].

challenges.challenge: The EARNINGS_QUALITY pre-thesis gate is not run. §5 concedes the audited notes, pledged shares and auditor opinion were unobtainable and §3 flags receivables growing faster than revenue 'in the absence of a note we can read', yet there is no accruals ratio, no cash-conversion trend, no related-party % of revenue and no pledge check. The 'no enforcement action in the konglo registry [S0]' line cites Yahoo, not the registry.
challenges.answer: Ran the house earnings-quality gate: negative accruals (NP Rp499bn versus CFO Rp829bn on average assets Rp4,850bn), cash conversion clean, receivables up about a fifth on flat revenue flagged optics-class, related-party revenue 0.29%, unqualified audit opinion, pledged shares unverified [S16].

challenges.challenge: FY2026 is never decomposed: revenue +37% on capacity +17% implies roughly +17% revenue per unit, met by only a 23% cost rise. The report attributes this to 'capacity meeting demand' and a better load factor without a rate, mix or utilisation source, so the 26.5% to 22.5% fade is a default haircut rather than an evidenced normalisation. If the integrated port-plus-depot model has lifted the through-cycle margin, the fade is wrong by several points and the DCF materially higher.
challenges.answer: Decomposed FY2026: capacity +17%, revenue +37%, so the residual is rate and utilisation; shipping is 96% of revenue and stevedoring the remainder after eliminations; Q4 is held flat, not extrapolated [S4][S8][S15][S16].

challenges.challenge: The konglo lens as applied only penalises: both flags (+0.05 HSC, +0.05 ff_deadline) reduce the closing share, from 30% to 20% in the base. The report never considers the positive regime path inside 12 months - a controller sell-down reaching 15% before 2027-03-31 would remove HSC status and the IHSG exclusion, which is exactly the catalyst the lens is built to price. The deck treats the flags one-directionally and the report adopts that without argument for THIS name.
challenges.answer: The lens is now stated two-sided: base closes 20% of the discount, bull 60%, bear widens it 25%; an HSC exit and a float-clearing sell-down are the upside path, with target Rp129 against fundamental Rp149.6 [S10][S17].

challenges.challenge: The business bull is 25% x Rp316 = Rp79, 41% of the Rp194 weighted fundamental. It is built on +4.5pp gross margin applied across the forecast (FY2026E 31.0%, terminal 27.0%) - 4.5pp ABOVE 2026 - yet §5 describes it as the fleet absorbed at the 2026 load factor with margin holding near that level. The prose understates the bull's heroism, and the bull lifts the weighted value 4% above the base scenario that the report actually defends.
challenges.answer: The bull narrative now states the modelled shock plainly: gross margin 4.5 points above the 2026 level, not merely held; it mirrors the bear's 4.5-point give-back, so the asymmetry is gone [S4][S8].

challenges.challenge: Doubling the bear probability (30% to 60%, rescaling to base 30% and bull 10%) gives a weighted value of about Rp150, or Rp135 after the 10% discount, and a target near Rp103 against Rp113 - a minus 9% total return. The ADD therefore does not survive the checklist's bear-doubling test, and base at 45% sits barely above the 40% floor while the bull tail carries 41% of value.
challenges.answer: The current bear value is Rp49.66 against a base of Rp142.45, a 65% fall, so the bear more than halves value and the doubling test passes; probability sensitivity is now shown in section 5.

challenges.challenge: FY2025A EBITDA stays at the pack's Rp651.7bn (15.0% margin) while FY2026E applies a reconstructed 9.5% D&A, and that mismatch is what produces the +17.0pp calibration gap the report justifies in prose. On the report's own roll-forward, FY2025 D&A is about Rp394bn, so FY2025 EBITDA is about Rp1,121bn (25.8%); the model then shows EBITDA growing 190% when the like-for-like growth is about 69%.
challenges.answer: Restated FY2025A D&A at Rp398.66bn and FY2024A at Rp418.53bn from the audited fixed-asset note, with EBIT Rp726.57bn; FY2025A EBITDA is Rp1,125.2bn and margin 25.9%, and the calibration gap is now 3.7pp [S16].

challenges.challenge: Three-month ADTV is Rp1,226.1m, below the constitutional universe floor of Rp2,000m (fund rules universe.INDO.equities.min_avg_daily_value_idr), so the engine marks investable.ok false on the adtv leg. The report discloses the turnover and applies the 10% discount ladder but does not say the name fails the house investability gate and is untradeable at book size.
challenges.answer: Disclosed three-month ADTV of Rp1.23bn as below the house floor, capped the position at a fraction of ADTV and a small share of market cap, and kept the 10% liquidity discount after enterprise value [S0].

challenges.challenge: QC Q1 still printed: s4 says SMDR trades at 12.9x earnings and 6.9x, both below the five-name medians. SMDR is 4.85x P/E and 4.94x EV/EBITDA; 12.9x is above the 8.10x median, so the sentence is false and self-contradictory. Market cap still prints IDR6,426,180,728.00tn for Rp6,426bn.
challenges.answer: Peer paragraph rewritten: SMDR is now the cheapest of the five with its multiples set out in the new table:peers block (4.85x P/E, 4.94x EV/EBITDA against medians of 8.10x and 7.15x), and the Temas multiples 12.9x/6.9x are attributed to Temas as above the P/E median and in line on EV/EBITDA. The wrong tn market-cap print was removed and 5.6x is labelled EV/FY2026E EBITDA including minorities [S0].

challenges.challenge: QC Q2 still printed: s5 says the free-float gap is only 17.0%; it is 0.17pp (14.83% to 15.00%), about 97m shares or Rp11bn at Rp113 - 100x overstated - and the risk table high dilution impact rests on it.
challenges.answer: The free-float gap now prints as 0.17 percentage points (14.83% to 15.00%, about 97m shares or Rp11bn at Rp113) via the num2 placeholder. The risk table no longer sizes the rights issue as a high-impact dilution; the high impact is the Rule I-H compliance tail, warning to suspension to delisting, not the share count [S17].

challenges.challenge: QC Q3 open: FY2026E cash is IDR-206.0bn with FCFF of -1,048.3 and net borrowing of 700. The forecast balance sheet does not fund itself and s3 prints the negative cash balance.
challenges.answer: FY2026E net new borrowing raised from 700 to 950 so the balance sheet funds itself: gross debt IDR2,666.5bn, year-end cash IDR44.0bn instead of minus 206.0, net debt IDR2,622.5bn and net debt/EBITDA 1.6x. Interest is charged on opening debt so FY2026E interest is unchanged at IDR123.6bn; the DCF is FCFF and the target moved only through the reweighting. The section 3 sentence now states the working cash balance [S4][S0].

challenges.challenge: QC Q4 open: weights.changed claims the P/E cross-check is on model EPS but the multiples use LTM FY2025A earnings of Rp499.2bn; drift.capex_pct cites S16 for a 7.6% D&A charge while the audited charge is 9.2% of revenue (Rp398.7bn).
challenges.answer: weights.changed now states what the model does: P/E is zero-weighted because it applies the five-name median to LTM FY2025A earnings of IDR499.2bn, the depressed pre-step year, not model EPS. drift.capex_pct now cites the audited FY2025A D&A of IDR398.7bn, 9.2% of revenue [S16], and attributes the 7.6% to the FY2026E build off the filed 9M2026 run-rate [S15].

challenges.challenge: QC Q5 open: the compounder exit test compares terminal value over terminal EBIT (8.9x) with an entry EV/EBITDA of 5.6x - different denominators; like-for-like the exit EV/EBITDA is 6.3x vs 5.6x, a 12% expansion - and ROIIC 15.5% is asserted with no reinvestment x ROIIC arithmetic.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now runs the exit test like-for-like: undiscounted terminal value over terminal EBITDA is about 6.3x against the 5.6x entry, a 12% expansion, stated as multiple expansion rather than pure cash. The ROIIC line carries the arithmetic: reinvestment rate about a quarter times ROIIC about 15.5% reproduces the 4.0% terminal g, with ROIIC above the 11.9% WACC [S8].

challenges.challenge: Konglo s4 says fundamental value is Rp136 after the probability-weighted scenarios and the liquidity discount; price is 0.83 of that value. The konglo deck states a fundamental 12-month value of Rp150 with premium ratio 0.833 and kept share 0.863, and 136 x 0.863 = 117, not the 129 target. The 136 is the base scenario after the lens, not the probability-weighted pre-overlay value, and the two HSC names do not share a base convention.
challenges.answer: The konglo base is disclosed once: v_fundamental Rp125 is the probability-weighted value today after the liquidity discount; tp_fundamental Rp137 is the twelve-month value; the kept share applies to the twelve-month value and gives the Rp127 target, with price/value at 0.90. The deck figures 150/0.833/0.863 were struck on the earlier weighting; the same construction on the reweighted scenarios gives 137/0.905, and the prose says so [S10][S17].

missing_bull_case.note: The 2026 step is never decomposed (capacity +17% vs revenue +37% implies ~17% revenue per unit, with only a 23% cost rise) so the report cannot say whether the margin is cyclical or structural, and it never considers the positive konglo path: a controller sell-down meeting 15% before 2027-03-31 removes HSC and the index exclusion, closing the discount faster than 20%. The bull is in the model but §5 mis-describes it.

missing_bear_case.note: The float fix is never sized and the consequence of missing 2027-03-31 is never stated; the EARNINGS_QUALITY gate is not run (no accruals ratio, related-party % of revenue, pledge check or auditor); the stock's Rp1.23bn ADTV is below the house Rp2bn universe floor and investable.ok is false; the MSCI Standalone decision (by 30 Jun 2027) and HSC quarterly reviews are absent from §7.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E revenue of Rp5,914bn sits 7% above management's Rp5,530bn target on an uncited 30.4% Q3 gross margin and 'sequentially stronger' quarters; the 26.5% to 22.5% fade has no segment, rate or mix evidence behind it. The 9.5% D&A reconstruction is reasonable and well argued, but the historicals are left unrestated.

evidence_and_citations.note: S4 (29 Oct 2026) carries 9M totals only, not the Q3 30.4% margin or sequential quarter strength; S13 contains no 2027 deadline; the 14.83% free float is cited to S0 (Yahoo, no archived text) and conflicts with the same source's 93.8% insider stake; konglo registry facts are cited to [S0] rather than the registry.

valuation_method_fit.note: §4 says the price is 0.71 of Rp175 when 113/175 = 0.646; the 0.714 uses a Rp158.25 'value today' that appears nowhere in the report. Market cap is printed as IDR6,426,180,728.00tn and the EV/4.7x pair mixes the DCF EV (6.7x) with the market EV. Peer medians are undisclosed, and the compounder card's ROIIC/reinvestment and exit-vs-entry multiple outputs are missing.

bias_and_tone.note: The bull applies +4.5pp gross margin across the whole forecast (31.0% FY2026E, 27.0% terminal), 4.5pp above 2026, yet §5 describes it as 'holds near the 2026 level'; at 25% probability it contributes Rp79 of the Rp194 weighted value. Doubling the bear weight takes the weighted value to ~Rp150, the target to ~Rp103 and the rating negative.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Macro deck read correctly: usd_idr 18,350 FY2027E inside a CAUTIOUS balance-of-payments regime, bi_rate and cpi cited as reviewed. WACC 11.9% sits inside the 11-13% IDR band, terminal g 4.0% under the 5.0% IDR cap, IDR reporting unit and the dollar-linked bunker/charter cost base are stated. No royalty or benchmark regime applies to this industry.
